title: Active & Passive Voice
summary: Two voice conversions per shift, built from an eight-row tense table and five named fault classes. Learn the table once — simple present to future perfect, being vs been slots, modal + be + V3, the Let-anchor for imperatives and By-whom order for questions — and both directions (active→passive, passive→active) become 25-second kills.

subtopics.title: Voice basics: the three moves
subtopics.concept:
Voice is a swap of stage positions: what received the action steps into the spotlight. **Three moves** convert any transitive sentence:

1. **Object becomes subject.** 'The chef *prepared* the meal' → '**The meal** …'
2. **Verb becomes be + V3**, with *be* carrying the original tense. Prepared (past) → **was** prepared; writes (present) → **is** written. The main verb is ALWAYS the past participle (V3) — never V1, never V2.
3. **Subject drops into a by-phrase** — and may vanish entirely when it is vague (someone, people, they) or unimportant: 'Someone has stolen my purse' → 'My purse has been stolen.'

**Pronoun cases swap too:** he↔him, she↔her, they↔them, I↔me, we↔us. 'He helps me' → 'I am helped by him.' In the options, a subject-slot *him* or an agent-slot *he* is an instant elimination.

**Only transitive verbs passivise.** Verbs without an object — *arrive, sleep, laugh, die, go* — have no passive at all. An option passivising 'The baby slept' does not exist in English, so the question never asks for one; but knowing this kills fake constructions in improvement items.

**The complete conversion table** — memorise as one block; every voice item is a row from it. Take the active sentence "She **writes** a letter":

| Tense | Active verb | Passive verb |
|---|---|---|
| Simple present | writes | is / are + V3 (a letter is written) |
| Present continuous | is writing | is / are being + V3 (is being written) |
| Present perfect | has written | has / have been + V3 (has been written) |
| Simple past | wrote | was / were + V3 (was written) |
| Past continuous | was writing | was / were being + V3 (was being written) |
| Past perfect | had written | had been + V3 (had been written) |
| Simple future | will write | will be + V3 (will be written) |
| Future perfect | will have written | will have been + V3 |
| Going to | is going to write | is going to be + V3 |

**Tenses with NO passive:** present perfect continuous (*has been writing*), past perfect continuous, future continuous (*will be writing*), and future perfect common usage limits. If the paper shows one of these, the conversion asks for the nearest allowed form — usually its simple counterpart. The 'being/been' skeleton is therefore: **be (in the tense of the main verb) + been (only after perfect or modal) + being (only after continuous or modal+be) + V3 always**.

tricks.title: Tense handover
tricks.body: The helping verb must reproduce the ORIGINAL tense: wrote→was, writes→is, will write→will be, has written→has been. Any tense change in the options is an error planted on purpose.

tricks.title: V3-only law
tricks.body: After be/been/being, the main verb is always V3 (written, given, built). 'Is wrote', 'was wrote', 'is build' are impossible — eliminate on sight.

tricks.title: Pronoun mirror
tricks.body: Subject pronoun moves to by-phrase in object case (he→by him); object pronoun moves to subject slot in subject case (me→I).

mistakes: Changing the tense while converting (writing 'is written' for 'wrote').
Keeping the active form in the by-phrase: 'by he' instead of 'by him'.
Forgetting that the object of a preposition can also passivise ('They laughed at him' → 'He was laughed at').
Trying to passivise intransitive verbs.
subtopics.notes:
### What voice means
In the **active voice** the subject does the action: *The chef prepared the meal.* In the **passive voice** the subject receives the action: *The meal was prepared by the chef.* Both sentences describe the same event — only the spotlight moves. Competitive exams (SSC, Railway, Banking) ask you to move that spotlight correctly, in under 30 seconds, twice per paper.

### The three moves — the whole method
1. **Object becomes subject.** Find the thing the verb acts on. In *The chef prepared the meal*, the meal is acted on, so *the meal* becomes the new subject.
2. **Verb becomes be + V3.** The main verb always turns into its past participle (V3: written, prepared, rung), and a helping verb *be* carries the original tense. *Prepared* is simple past, so *be* appears as *was*: *was prepared*. *Writes* is simple present, so *is written*. The tense never changes — only its carrier changes.
3. **Subject drops into a by-phrase.** The doer appears after *by*, in the object case: *by the chef, by him, by them*. When the doer is vague — *someone, people, they* — the by-phrase is usually dropped altogether.

Worked mini-example: *The postman rings the bell.* Object = the bell. Verb *rings* is simple present → *is rung*. Doer → *by the postman*. Result: *The bell is rung by the postman.*

### Pronouns swap their cases
Subject forms (I, he, she, we, they) become object forms (me, him, her, us, them) when they slide into the by-phrase. Object forms become subject forms when they move forward: *He helps me* → *I am helped by him*. Say the swap aloud once and the commonest option trap dies: *by he* and *us were invited* are impossible.

### Only transitive verbs can be passivised
A passive needs an object to promote. Verbs that take no object — *sleep, arrive, laugh, die, go, cry* — have no passive at all: *The baby slept peacefully* has no passive version, ever. This is a real exam type: *Select the sentence that cannot be changed into the passive voice* — the answer is the objectless verb. One refinement: verb + preposition can act as one transitive unit, so *They laughed at him* → *He was laughed at* is legal. Test the whole phrase, not the bare verb.

### The tense handover table (eight rows)
| Active | Passive |
|---|---|
| writes (simple present) | is / are + V3 |
| is writing (present continuous) | is / are being + V3 |
| has written (present perfect) | has / have been + V3 |
| wrote (simple past) | was / were + V3 |
| was writing (past continuous) | was / were being + V3 |
| had written (past perfect) | had been + V3 |
| will write (simple future) | will be + V3 |
| will have written (future perfect) | will have been + V3 |

Learn the rows as one block: the helping verb reproduces the original tense; the main verb is always V3. No row contains *is been*, *will being*, or a bare V1/V2 after *be*.

### Three instant elimination checks
1. **Tense changed?** *was written* offered for *wrote* — wrong.
2. **Wrong V-form after be?** *is wrote*, *is ringed*, *must obeyed* — wrong.
3. **Pronoun case broken?** *by he*, *us were invited* — wrong.
In a well-set item, each wrong option breaks exactly one of these rules; the correct option breaks none.

### Quick revision
- Three moves: object → subject; verb → be + V3 in the SAME tense; subject → by-phrase (dropped if vague).
- Pronoun mirror: he→him, she→her, they→them in the by-phrase; me→I when promoted to subject.
- No object → no passive: sleep, arrive, die, cry never passivise (but laugh AT him can).
- Vague agents (someone, they, people) usually vanish; the rest stay after by.
- Four fault classes to hunt in options: tense change, wrong V-form, missing being/been, pronoun case.

patterns.name: Three-move conversion with a pronoun swap
patterns.howToSpot: A short declarative stem; the options are passive versions differing in the verb skeleton or in by he/by him.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the object; promote it to subject.
2. Rebuild the verb as be + V3, keeping the original tense exactly.
3. Push the old subject behind by, in the object case.
4. Re-agree is/are/was/were with the NEW subject.

*Why it works:* every passive statement is built by these three moves and nothing else; the options differ only in which move was botched.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The peon rings the bell.*
example.solution: Object *the bell* → subject; *rings* (simple present) → **is rung**; doer → **by the peon**. Result: *The bell is rung by the peon.*

patterns.name: Vague agent drops out
patterns.howToSpot: The stem's subject is someone, people, they, one, or nobody-in-particular; the correct option carries no by-phrase while decoys drag 'by them/by people' along.
patterns.logic:
1. Check whether the doer names a specific person or thing.
2. Vague doers (someone, they, people) are dropped in the passive.
3. Keep the tense row untouched; the by-phrase is the only casualty.

*Why it works:* English omits agents that add no information; *My purse has been stolen* is idiomatic while *by someone* adds nothing.

example.q: Select the passive form: *Someone has switched off the fans.*
example.solution: Present perfect row → **have been switched off**; the vague agent *someone* is dropped: *The fans have been switched off.* Keeping 'by someone' is grammatical but never the keyed answer.

patterns.name: Pronoun-case elimination
patterns.howToSpot: The stem has pronouns on both sides (he...me, they...us) and the options tangle I/me, he/him, we/us in the two slots.
patterns.logic:
1. Decide each pronoun's NEW job: mover-to-by-phrase takes object case; promoted pronoun takes subject case.
2. Test each option's two pronoun slots independently — one correct slot does not save an option.
3. Reject any option whose verb also moved.

*Why it works:* *by he* and *me is helped* are impossible English, so case alone can finish the item.

example.q: Select the passive form: *They invited us to the wedding.*
example.solution: *We* is promoted (subject case, not *us*); *them* goes to the by-phrase: *We were invited to the wedding by them.*

patterns.name: No-passive filter (objectless or stative verb)
patterns.howToSpot: The stem asks which sentence CANNOT be passivised (or which CAN); the options mix transitive and objectless verbs.
patterns.logic:
1. Underline each option's verb and ask: does it act on a thing?
2. Sleep, arrive, die, cry, go, laugh (alone) have no object → no passive.
3. Stative verbs — have/own, resemble, lack, suit, cost — also refuse the passive in standard usage.

*Why it works:* the passive promotes an object; where no object exists, the promotion is impossible, and the setter builds the whole item on that fact.

example.q: Which cannot be changed into the passive voice: *The baby slept peacefully* / *The mother woke the baby* / *The doctor examined the reports* / *The nurse weighed the newborn*?
example.solution: *Slept* takes no object, so *The baby slept peacefully* has no passive. The other three all have objects (the baby, the reports, the newborn) and passivise cleanly.

subtopics.title: Tense-by-tense conversions in action
subtopics.concept:
Work one row at a time. For each, keep the tense and change only the verb skeleton:

| Active | Passive |
|---|---|
| Ram **writes** a story | A story **is written** by Ram |
| Sita **is drawing** a map | A map **is being drawn** by Sita |
| They **have caught** the thief | The thief **has been caught** |
| The cook **made** dinner | Dinner **was made** by the cook |
| The boys **were flying** kites | Kites **were being flown** by the boys |
| She **had finished** the work | The work **had been finished** by her |
| The PM **will address** the nation | The nation **will be addressed** by the PM |
| He **will have completed** it | It **will have been completed** |

**Number agreement restarts in the passive.** The new subject decides is/are, was/were, has/have: 'They have completed **the projects**' → '**The projects have** been completed' — the *has* of the active dies. SSC always plants one option that forgets to re-agree.

**The two 'being/been' positions:** continuous tenses take **being** (is being built, was being built); perfect tenses take **been** (has been taken, had been taken, will have been taken). Modals take plain **be**: will/can/must/should/may + **be** + V3. Any 'is been built' or 'will being taken' is impossible.

**Verb groups that resist the table:** *have/own/possess, resemble, lack, suit, fit, become* are normally stative — 'A car is had by him' is not English. When a stem uses these, expect a 'no passive possible' or a restructured answer, not a mechanical conversion.

tricks.title: Row-recall
tricks.body: Identify the active tense, then recite its passive row: present cont. → is/are being + V3; past perf. → had been + V3; future → will be + V3. Options break exactly one cell of the row.

tricks.title: Re-agreement sweep
tricks.body: After converting, make is/are/was/were/has/have agree with the NEW subject — check this before anything else.

tricks.title: being vs been slot
tricks.body: Continuous in the active → being. Perfect in the active → been. Modal → neither (plain be).

mistakes: Writing 'is been' for a continuous passive (correct: is being).
Writing 'is being' for a perfect passive (correct: has been).
Keeping the active subject as subject ('The cook was made dinner by…').
Forgetting by + object-case pronoun.
subtopics.notes:
### One row at a time
Every voice item is one row of the conversion table recited correctly. Identify the active tense, then produce its passive skeleton:

| Active | Passive | Example |
|---|---|---|
| writes | is / are + V3 | *Ram writes a story* → *A story is written by Ram* |
| is writing | is / are being + V3 | *Sita is drawing a map* → *A map is being drawn by Sita* |
| has written | has / have been + V3 | *They have caught the thief* → *The thief has been caught* |
| wrote | was / were + V3 | *The cook made dinner* → *Dinner was made by the cook* |
| was writing | was / were being + V3 | *The boys were flying kites* → *Kites were being flown by the boys* |
| had written | had been + V3 | *She had finished the work* → *The work had been finished by her* |
| will write | will be + V3 | *The PM will address the nation* → *The nation will be addressed by the PM* |
| will have written | will have been + V3 | *He will have completed it* → *It will have been completed* |

### The being/been slot rule
- **Continuous** in the active → **being**: *is being built, was being built, will be being built* (rare) — the word *being* only ever follows a continuous be or a modal's *be*.
- **Perfect** in the active → **been**: *has been taken, had been taken, will have been taken* — *been* only ever follows *have/had/will have*.
- **Modal** → plain **be**: *will be published, must be obeyed* — neither being nor been.

So *is been built* and *will being taken* are impossible; if an option contains them, kill it without reading further.

### Re-agreement: the new subject decides
After conversion, is/are, was/were, has/have must agree with the NEW subject, not the old one: *They have completed the projects* → *The projects **have** been completed* — the *have* of the active dies and *the projects* now govern. Setters plant one option that forgets to re-agree; sweep for it before anything else. *The clerk has filed the returns* → *The returns **have** been filed by the clerk* (not *has been*).

### Two nouns, two passives
Verbs that take two objects — *give, send, offer, grant, show, teach, tell, award* — produce two legal passives: *The teacher gave the students homework* → *The students were given homework* (person promoted) OR *Homework was given **to** the students* (thing promoted). The keyed answer usually promotes the person; the corrupted decoy drops the *to*: *Homework was given the students* is wrong.

### Tenses with no passive
Present perfect continuous (*has been writing*), past perfect continuous (*had been writing*) and future continuous (*will be writing*) have no passive row. When a stem uses one, the exam either avoids it or expects the nearest simple row. Do not invent *is being been written* — it does not exist.

### Stative verbs resist too
*A car is had by him* is not English. *Have/own/possess, resemble, lack, suit, fit, cost* normally refuse the passive. If a stem uses them, look for a *no passive possible* judgement rather than a conversion.

### Quick revision
- Perfect rows: has/have been, had been, will have been + V3. Continuous rows: is/are/was/were being + V3. Modals: be + V3, nothing between.
- being after continuous be; been after have/had; never is been, never will being.
- Re-agree with the NEW subject before checking anything else.
- Double-object verbs: person-promoted passive is keyed; the thing-promoted one must keep *to*.
- No passive: perfect continuous tenses; have/own/resemble/lack/suit.

patterns.name: Perfect-row passives (has/had/will have been + V3)
patterns.howToSpot: The active verb is has written / had written / will have written; the options differ in been, the auxiliary, or the tense.
patterns.logic:
1. Tag the active tense: present perfect, past perfect or future perfect.
2. Produce its row: has/have been + V3, had been + V3, will have been + V3.
3. Agree the auxiliary with the new subject; keep the by-agent in object case.

*Why it works:* the perfect rows are the most-set rows in the paper, and every wrong option breaks exactly one cell (been dropped, tense shifted, agreement lost).

example.q: Select the passive form: *The workers have painted the gate.*
example.solution: Present perfect → **has/have been + V3**; new subject *the gate* is singular: *The gate has been painted by the workers.*

patterns.name: Continuous-row passives (is/are/was/were being + V3)
patterns.howToSpot: The active verb is is writing / was writing type; options juggle being, been and the bare participle.
patterns.logic:
1. Continuous active → being row: is/are/was/were + being + V3.
2. Match was/were to the new subject's number.
3. Refuse *is been* and *is building*-type answers that drop the passive entirely.

*Why it works:* being is the continuous marker; the moment the active is continuous, the passive must show being — options without it are dead.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The masons are laying the bricks.*
example.solution: Present continuous → **are being laid**: *The bricks are being laid by the masons.* 'Are laid' would claim a habitual act, not an ongoing one.

patterns.name: Re-agreement with the new subject
patterns.howToSpot: The active subject is plural (they, the workers) and the promoted object is singular (the gate, the trophy) — or the reverse; one option agrees with the OLD subject.
patterns.logic:
1. Promote the object; note its number: singular or plural.
2. Choose is/was/has for a singular new subject; are/were/have for a plural one.
3. Only then check the rest of the row (been, V3, by-agent).

*Why it works:* the helping verb follows its own subject, which changed; options built from the old subject's number are the planted fault.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The clerk has filed all the returns.*
example.solution: New subject *the returns* is plural → **have been filed**: *The returns have been filed by the clerk.* 'Has been filed' agrees with the clerk, not with the new subject.

patterns.name: being vs been slot discrimination
patterns.howToSpot: The options are identical except for the being/been word — e.g. is being repaired vs is been repaired vs was being repaired.
patterns.logic:
1. Ask what the active tense is: continuous or perfect.
2. Continuous → being; perfect → been; modal → neither.
3. Check the auxiliary's tense matches the active exactly.

*Why it works:* being and been live in fixed slots; swapping them is the single most planted voice error in the paper.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The engineers were repairing the bridge when we crossed.*
example.solution: Past continuous → **was being repaired**: *The bridge was being repaired when we crossed.* 'Was been repaired' puts been in a continuous slot — impossible.

patterns.name: Double-object verb: person-promoted passive
patterns.howToSpot: The stem has a person and a thing after verbs like give, grant, show, offer, award; one correct option promotes the person, decoys corrupt the other passive.
patterns.logic:
1. Identify the indirect object (person) and direct object (thing).
2. The keyed passive usually promotes the person: person + was/were + V3 + thing + by-agent.
3. If an option promotes the thing instead, it must carry *to* before the person — without *to* it is broken.

*Why it works:* both passives are legal, but the person-promoted one needs no preposition, so the setter corrupts the thing-promoted one by deleting *to*.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The principal granted Meena a scholarship.*
example.solution: Person promoted: *Meena was granted a scholarship by the principal.* 'A scholarship was granted Meena' is broken — the thing-promoted version needs *to*: *granted **to** Meena*.

subtopics.title: Modals, imperatives, infinitives and questions
subtopics.concept:
**Modals:** will, shall, can, could, may, might, must, should, ought to → **modal + be + V3**.
'You must obey the rules' → 'The rules must be obeyed.' 'They can solve it' → 'It can be solved (by them).'

**Imperatives** convert with **Let**:
- Order: 'Shut the door' → 'Let the door be shut.'
- Advice: 'Help the poor' → 'Let the poor be helped.'
- Negative order: 'Do not touch the wire' → 'Let the wire not be touched' / 'The wire should not be touched.'
- Request with 'please': 'Please post this letter' → 'You are requested to post this letter.'

**Infinitives:** to write → **to be written** ('I want someone to write this' → 'I want this to be written'). **Gerunds:** writing → **being written** ('He likes people praising him' → 'He likes being praised').

**Questions:**
- **Who** asks → **By whom** + auxiliary + subject: 'Who wrote this?' → 'By whom was this written?' (The wh-word moves to front with *by whom*; the auxiliary then precedes the new subject — word order is the planted error.)
- **Whom/what** as object → normal passive with the wh-word as subject: 'Whom did you call?' → 'Who was called by you?' 'What did he buy?' → 'What was bought by him?'
- Yes/no questions keep inversion: 'Did she sing a song?' → 'Was a song sung by her?'

**Factitive and double-object verbs** (give, send, offer, teach, tell, show) have TWO passives: 'The teacher gave **the students** homework' → 'The students were given homework…' OR 'Homework was given to the students…'. Both are correct; papers use one as key and corrupt the other (dropping 'to' is the classic corruption).

tricks.title: Let-anchor
tricks.body: An imperative stem (no subject, base verb) signals the Let + object + be + V3 answer. Any option without 'Let' or a modal cannot be right.

tricks.title: By whom inversion
tricks.body: Who→questions convert to 'By whom + was/were/is + new subject + V3'. Check the word order first — options scramble it.

tricks.title: Request formula
tricks.body: Please → 'You are requested to …'; order → 'Let … be …'; advice → 'You are advised to …' or '… should be …'.

mistakes: Converting 'Please help me' to 'Let me be helped' instead of 'You are requested to help me'.
Writing 'By whom this was written?' — statement order in a question; it needs 'By whom was this written?'
Dropping 'to' in the second passive of a double-object verb ('Homework was given the students').
Using 'ought to be' wrongly as 'ought be' or 'ought to been'.
subtopics.notes:
### Modals: one row, no exceptions
Will, shall, can, could, may, might, must, should, ought to → **modal + be + V3**.
*You must obey the rules* → *The rules must be obeyed.* *They can solve it* → *It can be solved.* No *being*, no *been* after a modal: *must being obeyed* and *must been obeyed* are impossible. *Ought to* keeps its *to*: *The bill ought to be paid.*

### Imperatives: the Let anchor
An order has no subject and starts with a base verb. Convert with **Let + object + be + V3**:
- Order: *Shut the door* → *Let the door be shut.*
- Negative order: *Do not pluck the flowers* → *Let the flowers not be plucked* (or a modal version: *The flowers should not be plucked*).
- The verb after *be* is always V3: *Let the gate be opened*, never *be open* (adjective) or *be opening*.

### Requests, advice, warnings
The polite words change the skeleton, not the tense:
- **Please / kindly** → *You are requested to + V1*: *Please post this letter* → *You are requested to post this letter.*
- **Advice** (should/ought in sense) → *You are advised to + V1*: *Give up smoking* → *You are advised to give up smoking.*
- **Warning** (never, do not — danger) → *You are warned not to + V1.*
Learn the three openers as a chant: please → requested, advice → advised, danger → warned.

### Questions: three shapes
1. **Who** as doer → **By whom + auxiliary + subject + V3**: *Who broke the window?* → *By whom was the window broken?* Word order is the planted error: *By whom the window was broken?* is statement order, not question order.
2. **Whom/what** as receiver → the wh-word itself becomes the subject: *Whom did the manager appoint?* → *Who was appointed by the manager?* (whom becomes who in subject position).
3. **Yes/no question** → auxiliary first, new subject next: *Did she sing a song?* → *Was a song sung by her?*

### Infinitives and gerunds
- *to write* → **to be written**: *I want someone to compile the report* → *I want the report to be compiled.*
- *writing* (gerund) → **being written**: *He likes people praising him* → *He likes being praised.*
- After *likes, hates, remembers, wants* the being/to be forms are the keyed answers; decoys offer *been praised* (impossible after likes) or an active participle.

### Factitive and double-object verbs
*Give, send, offer, grant, show, teach, award* yield two passives (person-promoted and thing-promoted with *to*). *The guide showed the tourists the paintings* → *The tourists were shown the paintings by the guide* — clean; *The paintings were shown the tourists* — broken, needs *to the tourists*.

### Let me / Let us
- *Let us go* (suggestion) belongs to narration, not voice — do not force a Let-passive.
- *Let me sit here* (permission) → *I should be allowed to sit there* style answers; papers rarely test it in voice, more often in improvement.

### Quick revision
- Modal row: modal + be + V3 — no being, no been, no to (except ought to).
- Order → Let + object + be + V3; negative → Let ... not be ... or should not be.
- please → You are requested to; advice → You are advised to; danger → You are warned not to.
- Who-questions → By whom + aux + subject + V3; whom-questions → Who was V3 by ...?
- to write → to be written; people praising → being praised.

patterns.name: Modal + be + V3
patterns.howToSpot: The stem carries will/can/must/should/ought to; options scatter being, been, bare V1 or V3 after the modal.
patterns.logic:
1. Spot the modal; nothing between modal and be.
2. Fixed row: modal + be + V3 — no being, no been.
3. Keep the modal itself unchanged (must stays must; would for will is a decoy).

*Why it works:* the modal row has zero variants, so any option that inserts being/been or drops be is instantly wrong.

example.q: Select the passive form: *You should check the receipts.*
example.solution: Modal row: **should be checked** — *The receipts should be checked.* 'Should checked' loses be; 'should being checked' and 'should been checked' break the slot.

patterns.name: Imperative → Let + object + be + V3
patterns.howToSpot: The stem is a bare order starting with a base verb (Shut, Post, Switch off) and no subject; the right option starts with Let.
patterns.logic:
1. Recognise the imperative (no subject, base verb).
2. Skeleton: Let + object + be + V3.
3. Reject options without Let (statements) and options with V1/V-ing after be.

*Why it works:* Let is the standard passive carrier of a command; the exam always plants a statement-form decoy and a missing-be decoy.

example.q: Select the passive form: *Switch off the mobile.*
example.solution: Order → **Let the mobile be switched off.** 'Let the mobile switched off' drops be; 'The mobile is switched off' turns the order into a statement.

patterns.name: Negative imperative and warnings
patterns.howToSpot: The stem says Do not ... / Never ...; options must carry not in the right slot with the right skeleton (requested/advised/warned not to, or Let ... not be).
patterns.logic:
1. Classify the tone: polite request (please...not) → requested not to; advice → advised not to; warning → warned not to.
2. Bare negative order → Let + object + not + be + V3, or a modal version (should not be).
3. Check the negative word sits before to: *not to smoke*, never *to not smoke* in keyed answers.

*Why it works:* the negative travels with the reporting frame; options that drop the frame or misplace not fail at once.

example.q: Select the passive form: *Please do not smoke in the hall.*
example.solution: Polite negative request → *You are requested **not to smoke** in the hall.* The skeleton requested + not to + V1 keeps both the politeness and the prohibition.

patterns.name: Request formula: You are requested to
patterns.howToSpot: The stem contains please or kindly with a base verb; the keyed option begins You are requested to and decoys begin Let or use the noun request.
patterns.logic:
1. See please/kindly → the request frame: You are requested to + V1.
2. Keep the rest of the sentence word for word after to.
3. Let-forms and is + V3 statements are decoys for a please-sentence.

*Why it works:* please cannot survive inside a passive clause; English swaps it for the frame *you are requested to*, and the exam tests exactly that swap.

example.q: Select the passive form: *Kindly grant me a day's leave.*
example.solution: **You are requested to grant me a day's leave.** Nothing else changes: grant stays a base verb after to, and the listener's *me* is kept.

patterns.name: Question conversions (By whom / Who was)
patterns.howToSpot: The stem ends with a question mark; who-questions convert with By whom at the front, whom/what-questions promote the wh-word to subject.
patterns.logic:
1. Decide the wh-word's job in the question: doer (who) or receiver (whom/what).
2. Doer → By whom + auxiliary + new subject + V3 (+?).
3. Receiver → the wh-word itself is promoted: *Who was appointed by the manager?*
4. Check question word order — auxiliary BEFORE subject.

*Why it works:* question conversions fail on word order far more often than on verb form; checking the order first settles the item.

example.q: Select the passive form: *Who broke the window?*
example.solution: **By whom was the window broken?** — By whom + was (past of the do-broken frame) + the window + broken. 'By whom the window was broken?' is statement order; 'Who was broken the window?' scrambles the roles.

patterns.name: Infinitive and gerund passives (to be / being + V3)
patterns.howToSpot: The stem has to + verb after want/like/hate, or a gerund with people/someone as its doer (people praising him); options offer to be, being, been forms.
patterns.logic:
1. Infinitive: to + V1 → to + be + V3 (*to compile* → *to be compiled*).
2. Gerund: V-ing → being + V3 (*praising him* → *being praised*).
3. Reject been after like/want (been only follows have/had) and active forms that keep the old doer.

*Why it works:* the passive marker (be/being) slides into the same slot the non-finite verb occupied; the tense frame of the sentence never moves.

example.q: Select the passive form: *He likes people praising him.*
example.solution: Gerund passive: *He likes **being praised**.* 'Likes been praised' is impossible (been needs have/had); 'likes to praise' reverses the meaning.

subtopics.title: Reverse conversions: passive to active
subtopics.concept:
The reverse run appears in every shift. Move the by-agent (if any) into the subject slot, rebuild the tense from the passive skeleton, and give the old subject object position:

| Passive | Active |
|---|---|
| The letter **was written** by Sita | Sita **wrote** the letter |
| The road **is being repaired** | They **are repairing** the road |
| The work **had been finished** | She **had finished** the work |
| The results **will be declared** | The board **will declare** the results |
| The kite **was being flown** by the boy | The boy **was flying** the kite |

**Recover the tense from the FIRST auxiliary**, not the participle: was written → past simple (wrote); is being written → present continuous (is writing); has been written → present perfect (has written); had been written → past perfect (had written); will be written → future (will write).

**Missing agent:** when no by-phrase exists, supply *they/people/someone* — 'The thief was arrested' → 'They arrested the thief'. Papers accept the standard vague subject; the options differ only in verb form.

**Pronouns reverse too:** 'He was praised by them' → 'They praised **him**.' Watch the object case at the end — 'praised he' is the planted error.

**'Let' passives convert back to imperatives:** 'Let the door be shut' → 'Shut the door.'

tricks.title: First-auxiliary tense
tricks.body: Read only the first auxiliary to fix the tense: was→past, is→present, has/had→perfect, will→future, is being→present continuous, was being→past continuous.

tricks.title: Agent hunt
tricks.body: Find the by-phrase; that noun/pronoun becomes the subject. No by-phrase → they/people/someone.

tricks.title: Object-case exit check
tricks.body: The final pronoun must be in object case: 'They praised him', not 'he'. Many options fail exactly here.

mistakes: Taking 'was being chased' back to 'chased' (losing the continuous: were chasing).
Leaving the old subject in subject position ('The principal was praised him').
Ending with a subject-case pronoun ('praised he').
Changing tense on the way back (was written → has written).
subtopics.notes:
### The reverse run
Passive → active appears in every second paper. The method mirrors the forward one: promote the agent, rebuild the tense from the passive skeleton, demote the old subject.

| Passive | Active |
|---|---|
| The letter was written by Sita | Sita **wrote** the letter |
| The road is being repaired | They **are repairing** the road |
| The work had been finished | She **had finished** the work |
| The results will be declared | The board **will declare** the results |
| The kite was being flown by the boy | The boy **was flying** the kite |

### Read the FIRST auxiliary, not the participle
The participle (written, repaired) never tells you the tense — every row ends in V3. The first auxiliary carries the tense:
- was/were + V3 → simple past (*was written* → *wrote*)
- is/are being + V3 → present continuous (*is being written* → *is writing*)
- was/were being + V3 → past continuous (*was being written* → *was writing*)
- has/have been + V3 → present perfect (*has been written* → *has written*)
- had been + V3 → past perfect (*had been written* → *had written*)
- will be + V3 → simple future (*will be written* → *will write*)
- will have been + V3 → future perfect (*will have been written* → *will have written*)
- modal + be + V3 → modal + V1 (*must be obeyed* → *must obey*)

### The agent hunt
- A by-phrase gives the new subject: *by Sita* → Sita. Keep the noun exactly; change only its position.
- No by-phrase → supply the standard vague subject **they** (or people): *The thief was arrested last night* → *They arrested the thief last night.* Papers accept they; the options differ only in verb form.
- Do not promote a noun that was not the agent: *The window was broken by the cricketer* → *The cricketer broke the window*, never *The window broke the cricketer*.

### The object-case exit
The old subject leaves through the object slot in object case: *She was praised by the teacher* → *The teacher praised **her*** (not she). *He was helped by his friends* → *His friends helped **him***. Any option ending *praised she / helped he* is dead on arrival.

### Continuous skeletons must come back continuous
*was being + V3* is past CONTINUOUS — the active must be *was/were + V-ing*: *The path was being cleared by volunteers* → *The volunteers were clearing the path.* The commonest decoy returns a simple past (*cleared*) and loses the ongoing sense; a second decoy changes tense to present perfect. Refuse both.

### Let-passives reverse to orders
*Let the door be shut* → *Shut the door.* *You are requested to post this letter* → *Please post this letter.* Reverse the frame word as well: requested signals please, advised signals should-giving, warned signals danger.

### Quick revision
- Agent becomes subject; no agent → they.
- Tense from the FIRST auxiliary: was → past, is being → present continuous, has been → present perfect, had been → past perfect, will be → future, modal be → modal + V1.
- Old subject exits in object case: praised her, helped him.
- being skeleton → V-ing active; never return a simple past for it.
- requested → please, Let ... be → bare order.

patterns.name: Tense recovery from the first auxiliary
patterns.howToSpot: A be + V3 stem with a by-agent; the four active options differ in tense (has delivered / had delivered / is delivering / will deliver).
patterns.logic:
1. Ignore the participle; read the first auxiliary.
2. Map it: had been → had + V3; has been → has + V3; was being → was/were + V-ing; will be → will + V1.
3. Move the by-agent to the subject slot and demote the old subject.

*Why it works:* every passive row ends in V3, so only the auxiliary distinguishes the eight rows; reading it first fixes the tense in two seconds.

example.q: Select the active form: *The walls had been whitewashed by the masons.*
example.solution: had been + V3 → past perfect: *The masons **had whitewashed** the walls.* 'Have whitewashed' shifts to present perfect; 'were whitewashing' changes the aspect.

patterns.name: Missing agent: supply they
patterns.howToSpot: The passive has no by-phrase; the correct option begins with They (or People) and decoys use the old subject as doer or shift the tense.
patterns.logic:
1. Confirm no by-phrase exists.
2. Put the standard vague doer they before the rebuilt verb.
3. Demote the passive's subject to object position, keeping the tense row.

*Why it works:* English passives hide vague agents; converting back, they is the conventional stand-in, and the exam keys it every time.

example.q: Select the active form: *The results will be declared on Monday.*
example.solution: No agent → **They will declare the results on Monday.** will be + V3 → will + V1. 'The results will declare...' keeps the old subject as doer — reversed roles.

patterns.name: Object-case exit pronoun
patterns.howToSpot: The passive's subject is a pronoun (he, she, they, we); options end with the pronoun in both cases (praised her / praised she).
patterns.logic:
1. Move the by-agent to the front; rebuild the tense.
2. The old subject-pronoun leaves in OBJECT case: her, him, them, us.
3. Scan the tail of every option for the pronoun first — it eliminates fastest.

*Why it works:* case reversal is the mirror of the forward pronoun swap, and *praised she* is ungrammatical at a glance.

example.q: Select the active form: *She was praised by the teacher.*
example.solution: Agent first: *The teacher praised **her*** — was praised → praised (simple past), she → her (object case). 'Praised she' breaks the case; 'praises her' shifts the tense.

patterns.name: Continuous skeleton returns to V-ing
patterns.howToSpot: The stem is is/are/was/were being + V3; one option returns a plain past, another a perfect — only the V-ing option keeps the continuous.
patterns.logic:
1. Spot being → the active MUST carry V-ing.
2. Pick the auxiliary by tense: is being → is/are + V-ing; was being → was/were + V-ing.
3. Agree the new auxiliary with the agent's number (workers → were).

*Why it works:* being is the continuous marker in both voices; dropping it in the active silently changes the sentence's meaning, which the key never allows.

example.q: Select the active form: *The path was being cleared by the volunteers.*
example.solution: was being + V3 → **were clearing**: *The volunteers were clearing the path.* 'Were cleared' loses the ongoing sense; 'have cleared' changes the tense.

subtopics.title: Exam strategy: the 20-second conversion protocol
subtopics.concept:
Voice items are worth one mark each in under 30 seconds — the purest formula topic in the paper. The protocol:

1. **Tag the voice.** Active stem → build passive; passive stem → build active.
2. **Fix the tense.** From the first auxiliary (active) or skeleton (passive). Say the row aloud: 'was writing → was being + V3'.
3. **Move the parts.** Object↔subject; subject→by-phrase (or they/people); pronouns swap case.
4. **Re-agree the verb** with its new subject.
5. **Eliminate the four classic faults** in options: wrong V-form (V1/V2 after be), broken being/been slot, unchanged tense, pronoun case error. In a well-set item each wrong option carries exactly one of these faults.

**Distribution reality:** roughly one active→passive and one passive→active per Tier 1 shift; Tier 2 adds voice items inside error-spotting and cloze. Tenses drawn are usually simple present, simple past, present perfect, present continuous and modals — master those five rows first, then add the rest.

**Daily plan:** 10 conversions a day, alternating directions, written not spoken. After a week, recite the eight-row table from memory; after two, the item needs only the row-recall plus the elimination sweep. Target: 100% accuracy, 25 seconds per item.

tricks.title: Fault-class elimination
tricks.body: Every wrong option breaks exactly one rule: V-form, being/been, tense, agreement, pronoun. Name the fault — the option dies by its name.

tricks.title: Five-row priority
tricks.body: Master simple present, simple past, present perfect, present continuous, modals first — they cover 80% of paper items.

tricks.title: Write, don't speak
tricks.body: Voice errors live on paper. Convert in writing daily; the hand learns the skeleton faster than the ear.

mistakes: Rushing the re-agreement check after conversion.
Memorising conversions word-by-word instead of as tense rows.
Ignoring pronoun case at the ends of sentences.
Treating 'is been' as acceptable because it sounds like the continuous.
subtopics.notes:
### Why this is the cheapest topic in the paper
Voice items are worth one mark each in under 30 seconds, and every item is a row of one table. There is no inference, no vocabulary, no context — only the row and the three moves. With the eight rows memorised, the section becomes marks on demand.

### The 20-second protocol
1. **Tag the voice.** Active stem → build passive; passive stem → build active.
2. **Fix the tense.** From the first auxiliary (active) or the first auxiliary of the be + V3 skeleton (passive). Say the row aloud: *was writing → was being + V3*.
3. **Move the parts.** Object ↔ subject; subject → by-phrase (or they if missing); pronouns swap case.
4. **Re-agree the verb** with its NEW subject.
5. **Eliminate by fault class** — every wrong option in a well-set item breaks exactly one rule.

### The four fault classes (name them, kill them)
| Fault class | What it looks like | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Wrong V-form after be | V1 or V2 where V3 belongs | *is wrote*, *must obeyed*, *is ringed* |
| being/been slot broken | been after continuous be; being after have | *is been built*, *has being taken* |
| Tense change | row swapped to another tense | *was written* offered for *wrote*; *would be* for *will be* |
| Pronoun case / agreement | by he; us were; has been for a plural new subject | *The returns has been filed* |

A fifth, rarer fault: role reversal — *The judge was acquitted by the accused* for *The judge acquitted the accused*.

### Where the marks actually come from
Roughly one active→passive and one passive→active per Tier 1 shift; Tier 2 adds voice items inside error-spotting, cloze and sentence improvement. The tenses drawn are usually simple present, simple past, present perfect, present continuous and modals — master those five rows first, then add past perfect and future perfect. Imperatives (Let) and By-whom questions appear about once every two or three shifts.

### When two options both look clean
Compare them on ONE dimension at a time, in this order: (1) tense row, (2) being/been, (3) agreement with the new subject, (4) pronoun case, (5) agent kept or dropped. One of the two will break a dimension — the other survives. Never choose by what sounds smoother; sound is what the wrong options are engineered to exploit (*is been* sounds exactly like *is being* at speed).

### Daily drill that actually works
Ten conversions a day, written by hand, alternating directions: five statement rows, two modals, two imperatives, one question. After a week, recite the eight-row table from memory before starting. After two, run only the fault-class sweep on practice papers. Target: 100% accuracy, 25 seconds per item. Voice rewards drilling more than reading — errors live on paper, not in the ear.

### Quick revision
- Protocol: tag voice → fix tense row → move parts → re-agree → eliminate by fault class.
- Fault classes: wrong V-form, being/been slot, tense change, case/agreement, role reversal.
- Five-row priority: simple present, simple past, present perfect, present continuous, modals.
- Two clean options? Test one dimension at a time — tense first.
- Write daily; voice is a hand skill, not an ear skill.

patterns.name: One clean option: fault-class elimination
patterns.howToSpot: Four passive options for one stem; each wrong one breaks a different rule (V-form, being/been, tense) and only one is clean.
patterns.logic:
1. Build the correct row yourself BEFORE reading the options.
2. Scan options for the four faults: V-form, being/been, tense, agreement.
3. Name each option's fault; the option with no nameable fault is the answer.

*Why it works:* items are engineered as one clean + three single-fault options; naming faults is faster than admiring sentences.

example.q: Select the passive form: *They are constructing a new library.*
example.solution: Row: present continuous → **is being constructed**: *A new library is being constructed by them.* Decoys: is been constructed (slot), is constructing (active), was being constructed (tense).

patterns.name: Tense-trap discrimination among near-identical options
patterns.howToSpot: All four options share the same words and differ only in the auxiliary chain (is cooked / was cooked / has been cooked / is being cooked).
patterns.logic:
1. Fix the active tense first and say its row aloud.
2. Match the option whose auxiliary chain reproduces that row exactly.
3. Refuse rows that are grammatical but from a DIFFERENT tense — grammar is not the test, the row is.

*Why it works:* the setter builds three grammatical-looking rows from neighbouring tenses; only row-faithfulness separates them.

example.q: Select the passive form: *The peon was ringing the bell.*
example.solution: Past continuous → **was being rung**: *The bell was being rung by the peon.* 'Was rung' (simple past row) and 'is being rung' (present continuous row) are both grammatical — but from the wrong rows.

patterns.name: Identify the voice of a given sentence
patterns.howToSpot: The stem asks which sentence is in the passive (or active) voice; options are four complete sentences, usually about the same event.
patterns.logic:
1. Look for the be/have been + V3 skeleton → passive; plain V1/V2/V-ing with a doer before the object → active.
2. Continuous actives (was reading) are still ACTIVE — V-ing after be is not a passive.
3. A by-phrase confirms the passive but is not required (agents can be dropped).

*Why it works:* the item tests recognition, not conversion; the decoy is always the continuous active that superficially resembles a passive.

example.q: Which sentence is in the passive voice: *The window was broken by the cricketer* / *The cricketer broke the window* / *The cricketer was breaking the window* / *The cricketer has broken the window*?
example.solution: *The window was broken by the cricketer* — be + V3 with the receiver as subject. The others keep the cricketer as doer, so they remain active however their tenses differ.

patterns.name: Combined skeletons (modal + perfect, future perfect, question + perfect)
patterns.howToSpot: The stem stacks two features — will have written, must not violate, Who has written — so the answer needs two rules applied in order.
patterns.logic:
1. Peel the outer frame first: modal stays, perfect adds been, question adds inversion/By whom.
2. Rows: will have written → will have been + V3; must not violate → must not be + V3; Who has written → By whom has ... been written.
3. Apply pronoun and agreement checks last.

*Why it works:* stacked items are just two rows worn at once; solving the outer frame first prevents mid-sentence panic.

example.q: Select the passive form: *They will have published the magazine by March.*
example.solution: Future perfect row: **will have been published** — *The magazine will have been published by March.* 'Will be published' drops the perfect; 'will have published' keeps the active.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A declarative stem in the active voice with a transitive verb; the options are be + V3 skeletons that differ in the auxiliary chain, in being/been, or in agreement with the new subject.
pyqPatterns.approach: Name the active tense and say its passive row aloud (was writing → was being + V3). Promote the object to subject, rebuild the verb from the row, re-agree is/are/was/were/has/have with the NEW subject, and move the doer behind by in the object case. Then eliminate options by fault: wrong form after be, being/been swapped, tense row changed, agreement lost.

example.q: Select the passive form: 'The workers have painted the gate.'
example.solution: Present perfect row → has/have been + V3; new subject 'the gate' is singular: *The gate **has been painted** by the workers.* 'Have been painted' agrees with the old subject — the planted fault.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem already shows be/have been + V3 and asks for the active; the options differ in the active verb's tense (gave / has given / had given / gives).
pyqPatterns.approach: Ignore the participle — every passive row ends in V3. Read the FIRST auxiliary to fix the tense (had been → past perfect, was → simple past, is being → present continuous, will be → future). Promote the by-agent to subject; if there is no agent, start with They. Let the old subject exit in the object case (she → her, we → us).

example.q: Select the active form: 'The walls had been whitewashed by the masons.'
example.solution: had been + V3 → past perfect: *The masons **had whitewashed** the walls.* 'Have whitewashed' shifts the row to present perfect — the commonest decoy.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem is an order: a base verb with no subject ('Shut the door', 'Do not pluck the flowers'); the keyed option begins with Let.
pyqPatterns.approach: Use Let + object + be + V3 for the order; for a negative order put not after the object (Let the flowers not be plucked) or switch to a modal version (should not be plucked). Reject options without Let (they turn the order into a statement) and any form after be that is not V3.

example.q: Select the passive form: 'Switch off the mobile.'
example.solution: *Let the mobile **be switched off**.* 'Let the mobile switched off' drops be; 'The mobile is switched off' is a statement, not the order.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem carries please or kindly (request), advice in command form, or a warning (Do not drink and drive); the keyed option opens with You are requested / advised / warned.
pyqPatterns.approach: Swap the polite word for its frame — please/kindly → You are requested to, advice → You are advised to, danger → You are warned not to — and keep a base verb after to. The negative sits before to: requested **not to smoke**. Everything else in the sentence crosses unchanged.

example.q: Select the passive form: 'Please post this letter today itself.'
example.solution: *You are **requested to post** this letter today itself.* The letter cannot be made the requested party, and 'to posting' breaks the frame.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem ends with a question mark; who, whom or what leads it. The options differ mainly in word order (By whom was... vs By whom the... was) and in who/whom choice.
pyqPatterns.approach: Decide the wh-word's job first. Doer (who) → By whom + auxiliary + new subject + V3, with question order (auxiliary before subject). Receiver (whom/what) → the wh-word itself is promoted to subject: Who was appointed by the manager? Check the order before the verb — order faults outnumber verb faults here.

example.q: Select the passive form: 'Who broke the window?'
example.solution: *By whom **was the window broken**?* 'By whom the window was broken?' is statement order; 'Who was broken the window' scrambles who did what.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem's subject is someone, people, they or one; one option keeps 'by someone/by them' and the keyed one drops it; the rest of the sentence is identical.
pyqPatterns.approach: Vague agents add no information, so drop them; keep specific agents (the gardener, everyone, the committee). Dropping the agent never changes the tense row — convert first, drop last. If two options differ only in the by-phrase, the shorter (agent-less) one is keyed.

example.q: Select the passive form: 'Someone has switched off the fans.'
example.solution: *The fans **have been switched off**.* Present perfect row with the vague someone dropped; 'by someone' is grammatical but never the keyed answer.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Options identical except for the slot word: is being repaired / is been repaired / was being repaired — or the stem is continuous and one option lacks being altogether.
pyqPatterns.approach: being belongs only to continuous rows (is/are/was/were being + V3); been belongs only to perfect rows (has/have/had/will have been + V3); a modal takes plain be with neither. Fix the active tense first, then pick the slot word — never by ear, because is been and is being sound alike at speed.

example.q: Select the passive form: 'The engineers were repairing the bridge.'
example.solution: Past continuous → *The bridge **was being repaired*** — being marks the continuous; 'was been repaired' puts been in a continuous slot and is impossible.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Voice fault inside a sentence (error-spotting and improvement)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The item is not a conversion but a sentence with an embedded voice fault: is been built, must obeyed, by he, a plural new subject with has been, or a passive built from an objectless verb.
pyqPatterns.approach: Sweep for the four fault classes in order: (1) wrong verb form after be (V1/V2 where V3 belongs), (2) being/been in the wrong slot, (3) tense row changed or agreement lost with the new subject, (4) pronoun case or role reversal. The part that breaks a class is the error.

example.q: 'The new scheme has being launched / by the government / without much publicity.' Find the error.
example.solution: Present perfect needs been, not being: has **been** launched. 'Has being launched' puts being in a perfect slot — the classic voice fault.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The chef had prepared the meal.
options: The meal has been prepared by the chef.
The meal was prepared by the chef.
The meal had prepared by the chef.
The meal had been prepared by the chef.
solvedExamples.solution: Active tense = **past perfect** (had + V3). Its passive row is **had been + V3**: 'The meal had been prepared by the chef.' Option B shifts tense to present perfect; Option C drops to simple past; Option D loses 'been'.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Past perfect row: had + V3 → had been + V3. Tense never changes.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

They are building a new bridge.
options: A new bridge is building by them.
A new bridge was being built by them.
A new bridge is being built by them.
A new bridge is been built by them.
solvedExamples.solution: Present continuous → passive row **is/are being + V3**. The new subject 'a new bridge' is singular, so **is** being built. Option B commits the classic 'is been' error (been belongs to perfect tenses); C uses V1; D changes tense to past.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Continuous → being, never been: is being + V3.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

The thief was being chased by the police.
options: The police were chasing the thief.
The police were chased the thief.
The police was chasing the thief.
The police had chased the thief.
solvedExamples.solution: 'was being + V3' is the **past continuous passive** → active is **was/were + V-ing**. The new subject 'police' is plural → **were chasing**. Option B writes V2 after 'were'; C breaks number; D changes tense.
solvedExamples.shortcut: was being + V3 → were + V-ing (past continuous back-conversion).

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

She writes a letter.
options: A letter is wrote by her.
A letter was written by her.
A letter is being written by her.
A letter is written by her.
practice.solution: Simple present → **is/are + V3**. 'A letter is written by her.' B uses V2 ('wrote') after is; C changes tense to past; D changes aspect to continuous.
practice.shortcut: Simple present row: is/are + V3.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The gardener is watering the plants.
options: The plants are watered by the gardener.
The plants are being watered by the gardener.
The plants are being water by the gardener.
The plants is being watered by the gardener.
practice.solution: Present continuous → **are being + V3** with the plural new subject 'the plants'. B uses V1; C fails number agreement (is for plants); D drops 'being', turning it into simple present.
practice.shortcut: are being + V3 — check the V3 and the number both.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

They have completed the project.
options: The project has completed by them.
The project has being completed by them.
The project have been completed by them.
The project has been completed by them.
practice.solution: Present perfect → **has/have been + V3**. The new subject 'the project' is singular → **has been completed**. B drops 'been'; C wrongly uses 'being' in a perfect slot; D agrees the verb with 'they' instead of the new subject.
practice.shortcut: Perfect row: has/have been + V3; agree with the NEW subject.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Someone has stolen my purse.
options: My purse has stolen.
My purse was stolen by someone.
My purse is stolen by someone.
My purse has been stolen.
practice.solution: Present perfect passive: 'My purse has been stolen.' The vague agent **someone** is dropped. B misses 'been'; C and D change the tense.
practice.shortcut: Vague agents (someone/they) vanish in the passive.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Open the gate.
options: Let the gate be open.
Let the gate be opened.
The gate is opened.
The gate be opened.
practice.solution: An imperative converts with **Let + object + be + V3**: 'Let the gate be opened.' B produces a statement, not an order; C lacks the auxiliary; D uses the adjective 'open' instead of V3 'opened'.
practice.shortcut: Imperative anchor: Let + object + be + V3.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

You must obey the rules.
options: The rules must being obeyed.
The rules must be obeyed.
The rules must be obey.
The rules must been obeyed.
practice.solution: Modal row: **modal + be + V3** — 'The rules must be obeyed.' B uses V1; C uses 'been' after a modal (been only follows have/will have); D uses 'being' where plain 'be' is required.
practice.shortcut: Modal row: modal + be + V3 — no being, no been.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Who taught you English?
options: By whom were you taught English?
Who was taught you English?
By whom you were taught English?
Whom were taught English by you?
practice.solution: Who-questions passivise to **By whom + auxiliary + subject**: 'By whom were you taught English?' B keeps 'who' instead of 'by whom'; C uses statement word order; D scrambles the clause entirely.
practice.shortcut: Who → By whom + aux + subject; word order is the trap.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

The novel was written by Premchand.
options: Premchand was written the novel.
Premchand has written the novel.
Premchand had written the novel.
Premchand wrote the novel.
practice.solution: 'was written' → simple past active: **wrote**. B keeps the passive verb; C and D both shift the tense (present perfect, past perfect).
practice.shortcut: was + V3 → past simple (V2).

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

The letter will be posted by the clerk.
options: The clerk will be posting the letter.
The clerk would post the letter.
The clerk will post the letter.
The clerk will posted the letter.
practice.solution: 'will be + V3' → future simple active: **will post**. B uses V2 after will; C keeps passive 'be' inside the active; D shifts the modal.
practice.shortcut: will be + V3 → will + V1.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

He was praised by the principal.
options: The principal praises him.
The principal praised him.
The principal praised he.
The principal was praised him.
practice.solution: Agent → subject ('the principal'); 'was praised' → simple past **praised**; old subject moves to object case: **him**. B ends in subject-case 'he'; C keeps the passive 'was'; D changes tense to present.
practice.shortcut: By-agent becomes subject; final pronoun in object case.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The teacher gave the students homework.
options: The students were given homework by the teacher.
The students was given homework by the teacher.
The homework was given the students by the teacher.
The students are given homework by the teacher.
practice.solution: Double-object verb: either object can lead. 'The students were given homework by the teacher' is correct (plural → were). B breaks number; C drops the preposition 'to' ('given the students' needs 'given to the students'); D changes tense.
practice.shortcut: give offers two passives; the indirect-object one keeps 'were given'.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The committee will announce the results.
options: The results will being announced by the committee.
The results would be announced by the committee.
The results will be announced by the committee.
The results will announced by the committee.
practice.solution: Simple future → **will be + V3**. B loses 'be'; C uses 'being' after a modal; D shifts the modal (would).
practice.shortcut: Future row: will be + V3.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

The road is being repaired by the workers.
options: The workers is repairing the road.
The workers have repaired the road.
The workers are repairing the road.
The workers are repaired the road.
practice.solution: 'is being + V3' → present continuous: **are repairing** (plural subject). B writes V3 after are; C fails number; D changes tense to perfect.
practice.shortcut: is being + V3 → are + V-ing.

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

Please help the poor.
options: The poor are helped.
You are request to help the poor.
You are requested to help the poor.
Let the poor helped.
practice.solution: A 'please' request converts to **You are requested to + V1**. B drops 'be' in the Let-form and loses the request tone; C gives a statement of fact; D writes the noun 'request' where V3 'requested' is needed.
practice.shortcut: please → You are requested to …; order → Let … be …

practice.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in passive voice.

The gardener had planted the saplings.
options: The saplings have been planted by the gardener.
The saplings had planted by the gardener.
The saplings were planted by the gardener.
The saplings had been planted by the gardener.
practice.solution: Past perfect → **had been + V3**: 'The saplings had been planted by the gardener.' B shifts to present perfect; C drops 'been'; D drops to simple past.
practice.shortcut: had + V3 → had been + V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The gardener waters the plants every morning.'
options: The plants are watering by the gardener every morning.
The plants were watered by the gardener every morning.
The plants have watered by the gardener every morning.
The plants are watered by the gardener every morning.
practice.solution: Simple present row → **are + V3**: the object *the plants* becomes the subject, *waters* becomes **are watered**, and the doer moves behind **by**. 'Are watering' keeps the active form; 'were watered' shifts the tense; 'have watered' drops *been*.
practice.shortcut: Row chant: waters → is/are watered. Then swap and add by.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The children are making a noise in the class.'
options: A noise is been made by the children in the class.
A noise is being made by the children in the class.
A noise is making by the children in the class.
A noise was being made by the children in the class.
practice.solution: Present continuous row → **is being + V3**: *a noise* is promoted, *are making* becomes **is being made** (the new subject is singular), and *the children* takes **by**. 'Is been made' puts been in a continuous slot; 'is making' stays active; 'was being made' changes the tense.
practice.shortcut: Active -ing → passive being + V3. Been never follows a continuous be.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The judge acquitted the accused of all charges.'
options: The judge was acquitted of all charges by the accused.
The accused is acquitted of all charges by the judge.
The accused was acquitted of all charges by the judge.
The accused had acquitted of all charges by the judge.
practice.solution: *The accused* is the receiver, so it becomes the subject: **was acquitted of all charges by the judge**. Promoting *the judge* instead reverses the roles of the courtroom; 'is acquitted' changes the tense; 'had acquitted' drops *been*.
practice.shortcut: Promote the RECEIVER, never the doer.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Someone has plucked my roses.'
options: My roses have been plucked.
My roses have been plucked by someone.
My roses has been plucked.
My roses had been plucked.
practice.solution: Present perfect row → **have been + V3**, and the vague agent *someone* is dropped: *My roses have been plucked.* The keyed answer never drags 'by someone' along; 'has been plucked' fails to agree with the plural *roses*; 'had been plucked' shifts to past perfect.
practice.shortcut: someone/they/people vanish in the passive.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'People speak Hindi all over northern India.'
options: Hindi is spoken by people all over northern India.
Hindi was spoken all over northern India.
Hindi is spoken all over northern India.
Hindi is speak all over northern India.
practice.solution: The vague doer *people* is dropped: **Hindi is spoken all over northern India.** Keeping 'by people' is the classic planted extra; 'was spoken' changes the tense; 'is speak' uses V1 where V3 belongs.
practice.shortcut: People as doer → drop it, convert, done.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'They will cancel the match if it rains.'
options: The match will be cancel if it rains.
The match will be cancelled if it rains.
The match would be cancelled if it rains.
The match will been cancelled if it rains.
practice.solution: Future row: **will be + V3** — *The match will be cancelled if it rains.* The vague *they* disappears; the if-clause stays untouched. 'Will be cancel' lacks the participle; 'would be cancelled' downgrades the modal; 'will been cancelled' breaks the slot (been never follows a bare modal).
practice.shortcut: Modal row: modal + be + V3. Nothing between modal and be.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'He teaches us grammar.'
options: Us are taught grammar by him.
We are taught grammar by him.
We are taught grammar by he.
We are teach grammar by him.
practice.solution: The receiver *us* is promoted to the subject form **we**, and the doer *he* slips into object case behind **by him**: *We are taught grammar by him.* 'Us are taught' keeps object case in the subject slot; 'by he' refuses the case swap; 'are teach' drops the participle.
practice.shortcut: Subject and by-agent swap cases: us→we, he→him.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'They have elected him president.'
options: He has been elected president by them.
He has been elected president.
Him has been elected president.
He has been elect president.
practice.solution: Present perfect row with the vague *they* dropped: **He has been elected president.** The pronoun *him* is promoted to subject case **he**. 'By them' is the planted vague agent; 'Him has been elected' keeps object case in the subject slot; 'has been elect' lacks the participle.
practice.shortcut: Promoted pronoun takes subject case: him→he.

practice.q: Which one of the following sentences CANNOT be changed into the passive voice?
options: The mother sang a lullaby.
The nurse fed the baby.
The baby slept peacefully on the cot.
The father bought a cradle.
practice.solution: *Slept* takes no object — there is nothing to promote, so *The baby slept peacefully on the cot* has no passive at all. The other three sentences each carry an object (*a lullaby*, *the baby*, *a cradle*) and convert cleanly.
practice.shortcut: No object → no passive. Test the verb, not the looks.

practice.q: Which one of the following sentences cannot be converted into the passive voice?
options: My uncle owns two flats in Pune.
My uncle has sold a flat in Pune.
My uncle is renting out a flat in Pune.
My uncle built two flats in Pune.
practice.solution: *Own* is a verb of possession; English does not passivise it — there is no accepted '*Two flats are owned by my uncle*'. *Sell*, *rent out* and *build* are action verbs with objects, so the other three sentences passivise normally.
practice.shortcut: Have/own/possess/resemble/lack/suit → no passive.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The students have cleaned the auditorium.'
options: The auditorium have been cleaned by the students.
The auditorium has being cleaned by the students.
The auditorium is cleaned by the students.
The auditorium has been cleaned by the students.
practice.solution: Present perfect row → **has/have been + V3**; the new subject *the auditorium* is singular, so **has been cleaned by the students**. 'Have been cleaned' agrees with the old subject; 'has being cleaned' puts being in a perfect slot; 'is cleaned' switches to the simple present row.
practice.shortcut: Perfect active → has/have been + V3. Agree with the NEW subject.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The hunters had trapped the leopard before dawn.'
options: The leopard has been trapped by the hunters before dawn.
The leopard had being trapped by the hunters before dawn.
The leopard had been trapped by the hunters before dawn.
The leopard was trapped by the hunters before dawn.
practice.solution: Past perfect row → **had been + V3**: *The leopard had been trapped by the hunters before dawn.* 'Has been trapped' lifts the row to present perfect; 'had being trapped' inserts being into a perfect slot; 'was trapped' drops to the simple past row.
practice.shortcut: had + V3 → had been + V3. The had never moves.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The chef is preparing a special dish for the guests.'
options: A special dish is prepared by the chef for the guests.
A special dish is been prepared by the chef for the guests.
A special dish is being prepared by the chef for the guests.
A special dish was being prepared by the chef for the guests.
practice.solution: Present continuous row → **is being + V3**: *A special dish is being prepared by the chef for the guests.* 'Is prepared' turns the ongoing act into a habit; 'is been prepared' breaks the continuous slot; 'was being prepared' shifts the row to past continuous.
practice.shortcut: Active is + V-ing → passive is being + V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The farmers were harvesting the paddy when it began to rain.'
options: The paddy was harvested by the farmers when it began to rain.
The paddy was being harvested by the farmers when it began to rain.
The paddy is being harvested by the farmers when it began to rain.
The paddy was being harvest by the farmers when it began to rain.
practice.solution: Past continuous row → **was being + V3**: *The paddy was being harvested by the farmers when it began to rain.* 'Was harvested' loses the ongoing sense; 'is being harvested' jumps tenses mid-sentence; 'was being harvest' lacks the participle.
practice.shortcut: were + V-ing → was/were being + V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The mayor has inaugurated the new flyovers.'
options: The new flyovers has been inaugurated by the mayor.
The new flyovers have been inaugurated by the mayor.
The new flyovers have being inaugurated by the mayor.
The new flyovers had been inaugurated by the mayor.
practice.solution: The new subject *the new flyovers* is plural, so the perfect row reads **have been inaugurated by the mayor**. 'Has been inaugurated' copies the old subject's number; 'have being inaugurated' breaks the slot; 'had been inaugurated' changes the tense.
practice.shortcut: After promoting, re-agree: flyovers → have, not has.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The committee has approved these proposals.'
options: These proposals has been approved by the committee.
These proposals have approved by the committee.
These proposals were approved by the committee.
These proposals have been approved by the committee.
practice.solution: New subject *these proposals* is plural → **have been approved by the committee**. 'Has been approved' forgets to re-agree; 'have approved by' drops *been*; 'were approved' moves the row to the simple past.
practice.shortcut: Plural new subject → have been, never has been.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The mechanics were repairing my scooter.'
options: My scooter was been repaired by the mechanics.
My scooter was being repaired by the mechanics.
My scooter is being repaired by the mechanics.
My scooter was repairing by the mechanics.
practice.solution: Past continuous row → **was being repaired by the mechanics** — being marks the continuous, been never does. 'Was been repaired' swaps the slot word; 'is being repaired' leaves the past; 'was repairing' keeps the active verb.
practice.shortcut: being = continuous, been = perfect. Fix the word first.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Someone is auditing our accounts this week.'
options: Our accounts are been audited this week.
Our accounts are auditing this week.
Our accounts were being audited this week.
Our accounts are being audited this week.
practice.solution: Present continuous row with the vague *someone* dropped: **Our accounts are being audited this week.** 'Are been audited' misplaces been; 'are auditing' leaves the sentence active with the accounts doing the auditing; 'were being audited' shifts to the past row.
practice.shortcut: Continuous active → being + V3; drop the vague agent.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The bank offered the farmer a loan.'
options: A loan was offered the farmer by the bank.
The farmer was offered a loan by the bank.
The farmer was offer a loan by the bank.
The bank was offered a loan by the farmer.
practice.solution: The person-promoted passive is keyed: *The farmer was offered a loan by the bank.* The thing-promoted version must insert *to* ('a loan was offered **to** the farmer'); without *to* it is broken. 'Was offer a loan' lacks the participle; promoting the bank reverses who offered what.
practice.shortcut: Person promoted = no preposition. Thing promoted = needs to.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The principal awarded the topper a gold medal.'
options: A gold medal was awarded the topper by the principal.
The topper was awarded a gold medal by the principal.
The topper was awarding a gold medal by the principal.
A gold medal was awarded by the topper to the principal.
practice.solution: Promote the person: *The topper was awarded a gold medal by the principal.* The medal-promoted option is missing *to* before the topper; 'was awarding' is the wrong form after was; making the medal awarded by the topper reverses the ceremony.
practice.shortcut: Award/give/show/offer: promote the person.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'You must complete the formalities today.'
options: The formalities must been completed today.
The formalities must be completed today.
The formalities must being completed today.
The formalities must be complete today.
practice.solution: Modal row: **must + be + V3** — *The formalities must be completed today.* Nothing may sit between the modal and be: no been, no being. 'Must be complete' uses the adjective instead of the participle, so the action disappears.
practice.shortcut: Modal + be + V3, nothing else in between.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'We should respect our elders.'
options: Our elders should been respected.
Our elders should respected.
Our elders should be respected.
Our elders would be respected.
practice.solution: **Our elders should be respected** — the modal *should* is kept exactly, be follows it, and the participle closes. 'Should respected' drops be; 'would be respected' swaps the modal itself, which the key never allows.
practice.shortcut: Keep the modal, add be, close with V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Shut the door.'
options: Let the door be shut.
Let the door shut.
The door is shut.
Let the door been shut.
practice.solution: An order converts with **Let + object + be + V3**: *Let the door be shut.* 'Let the door shut' drops be and reads as an active permission; 'The door is shut' is a plain statement, not the order; 'been shut' cannot follow let.
practice.shortcut: Order → Let + object + be + V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Do not pluck the flowers in the park.'
options: The flowers are not plucked in the park.
Let the flowers not plucked in the park.
Let the flowers not be plucked in the park.
Let the flowers not being plucked in the park.
practice.solution: Negative order → **Let + object + not + be + V3**: *Let the flowers not be plucked in the park.* 'Are not plucked' turns the order into a statement; 'not plucked' drops be; 'not being plucked' breaks the slot after let.
practice.shortcut: Negative order: Let ... not be + V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Please do not touch the exhibits.'
options: You are requested not to touch the exhibits.
