The exhibits are requested not to be touched.
You are requested to touch not the exhibits.
You are request not to touch the exhibits.
practice.solution: A polite please-sentence takes the frame **You are requested not to + V1**: *You are requested not to touch the exhibits.* Making the exhibits the requested party garbles the frame; 'to touch not' misplaces the negative; 'are request' drops the -ed.
practice.shortcut: please + not → requested not to + V1.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Never tell a lie.'
options: You are advise not to tell a lie.
You are advised not to tell a lie.
You are advised not telling a lie.
A lie is advised not to be told.
practice.solution: Advice in imperative form converts to **You are advised not to + V1**: *You are advised not to tell a lie.* 'Are advise' lacks the participle; 'not telling' replaces the infinitive with a gerund; the lie cannot be the subject of an advice frame.
practice.shortcut: Advice imperative → advised not to + V1.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Please post this letter today itself.'
options: You are requested that post this letter today itself.
This letter is requested to post today itself.
You are requested to post this letter today itself.
You are request to post this letter today itself.
practice.solution: **You are requested to post this letter today itself.** The frame requested + to + V1 swallows the please, and the rest of the sentence is carried across word for word. A that-clause after requested is ungrammatical; making the letter the requested party scrambles the frame.
practice.shortcut: Please ... → You are requested to + V1.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Kindly send the invitation card by this evening.'
options: The invitation card is requested to be sent by this evening.
You are requested to sending the invitation card by this evening.
You are requested to send the invitation card by this evening.
You are request to send the invitation card by this evening.
practice.solution: Kindly marks a request: **You are requested to send the invitation card by this evening.** The card cannot be the requested party; after to the base verb *send* is fixed — 'to sending' breaks the frame; 'are request' loses the -ed.
practice.shortcut: kindly = please → requested to + V1.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the question: 'Who invented the radio?'
options: By whom the radio was invented?
By whom was the radio invented?
Who was the radio invented?
Whom was invented the radio?
practice.solution: Who as doer → **By whom + auxiliary + subject + V3**: *By whom was the radio invented?* 'By whom the radio was invented?' is statement order — the auxiliary must precede the subject in a question; 'Who was the radio invented' scrambles the roles.
practice.shortcut: Who-questions: By whom + aux + subject + V3 + ?

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the question: 'Whom has the principal punished?'
options: Who has been punished by the principal?
Who has punished by the principal?
Who has been punish by the principal?
By whom has the principal been punished?
practice.solution: Here whom is the receiver, so the wh-word itself is promoted to subject: **Who has been punished by the principal?** — present perfect row, been + punished. 'Has punished' drops been; 'been punish' lacks the participle; the last option makes the principal the punished party.
practice.shortcut: Whom-receiver questions: the wh-word becomes the subject.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'I want someone to type this letter at once.'
options: I want this letter to been typed at once.
I want this letter being typed at once.
I want this letter to type at once.
I want this letter to be typed at once.
practice.solution: Infinitive passive: **to be + V3** — *I want this letter to be typed at once.* The vague *someone* disappears. 'To been typed' is impossible (been needs have/had); 'being typed' replaces the infinitive with a gerund; 'to type' leaves the letter typing itself.
practice.shortcut: to + V1 → to be + V3 after want.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'She hates people criticising her openly.'
options: She hates been criticised openly.
She hates to criticising openly.
She hates people criticised openly.
She hates being criticised openly.
practice.solution: Gerund passive: **being + V3** — *She hates being criticised openly.* 'Been criticised' is impossible after hates (been only follows have/had); 'to criticising' mixes the infinitive marker with a gerund; keeping people leaves the clause active.
practice.shortcut: people + V-ing → being + V3 after like/hate.

practice.q: Select the correct active form of the sentence: 'A splendid farewell was given to the retiring officer by the staff.'
options: The staff has given a splendid farewell to the retiring officer.
The staff had given a splendid farewell to the retiring officer.
The staff gave a splendid farewell to the retiring officer.
The staff gives a splendid farewell to the retiring officer.
practice.solution: The first auxiliary *was* fixes the simple past: **The staff gave a splendid farewell to the retiring officer.** 'Has given' lifts the row to present perfect; 'had given' to past perfect; 'gives' to the present.
practice.shortcut: Read the FIRST auxiliary for the tense, ignore the V3.

practice.q: Select the correct active form of the sentence: 'The missing file had been traced by the intern.'
options: The intern has traced the missing file.
The intern had traced the missing file.
The intern traced the missing file.
The intern was tracing the missing file.
practice.solution: had been + V3 → past perfect: **The intern had traced the missing file.** 'Has traced' swaps the auxiliary; 'traced' alone drops the earlier-of-two sense the past perfect carries; 'was tracing' changes the aspect.
practice.shortcut: had been + V3 → had + V3. The had survives.

practice.q: Select the correct active form of the sentence: 'The culprit will be arrested soon.'
options: The culprit will arrest soon.
They will arrested the culprit soon.
They will arrest the culprit soon.
They would arrest the culprit soon.
practice.solution: No by-agent, so the standard vague doer **they** steps in: *They will arrest the culprit soon.* — will be + V3 becomes will + V1. 'The culprit will arrest' promotes the receiver as doer; 'will arrested' breaks the form after will; 'would' downgrades the modal.
practice.shortcut: No agent → start with They, keep the modal.

practice.q: Select the correct active form of the sentence: 'The old bridge has been declared unsafe.'
options: They had declared the old bridge unsafe.
They have declared the old bridge unsafe.
They has declared the old bridge unsafe.
They are declaring the old bridge unsafe.
practice.solution: has been + V3 → present perfect with the vague doer: **They have declared the old bridge unsafe.** 'Had declared' shifts to past perfect; 'has declared' fails to agree with they; 'are declaring' changes the aspect.
practice.shortcut: has/have been + V3 → they have + V3.

practice.q: Select the correct active form of the sentence: 'He was honoured by the university at its convocation.'
options: The university honoured he at its convocation.
The university has honoured him at its convocation.
He honoured the university at its convocation.
The university honoured him at its convocation.
practice.solution: The by-agent becomes the subject and the old subject exits in object case: *The university honoured **him** at its convocation.* 'Honoured he' refuses the case swap; 'has honoured' adds an auxiliary the simple past never had; making him the honouree reverses the event.
practice.shortcut: Promoted-out pronoun takes object case: he→him.

practice.q: Select the correct active form of the sentence: 'We were led into the hall by the usher.'
options: The usher led us into the hall.
The usher led we into the hall.
The usher has led us into the hall.
We led the usher into the hall.
practice.solution: **The usher led us into the hall** — the by-agent leads, and *we* becomes **us** in the object slot. 'Led we' keeps subject case where an object belongs; 'has led' invents a perfect; 'We led the usher' reverses who followed whom.
practice.shortcut: we→us when it leaves the subject seat.

practice.q: Select the correct active form of the sentence: 'A new flyover is being built near the market.'
options: They are building a new flyover near the market.
They build a new flyover near the market.
They have built a new flyover near the market.
They were building a new flyover near the market.
practice.solution: is being + V3 is the present continuous row: **They are building a new flyover near the market.** 'Build' drops the continuous; 'have built' jumps to the perfect; 'were building' drifts into the past.
practice.shortcut: being in the passive → V-ing in the active.

practice.q: Select the correct active form of the sentence: 'The damaged goods were being unloaded by the dockworkers.'
options: The dockworkers unloaded the damaged goods.
The dockworkers were unloaded the damaged goods.
The dockworkers have unloaded the damaged goods.
The dockworkers were unloading the damaged goods.
practice.solution: were being + V3 → past continuous: **The dockworkers were unloading the damaged goods.** 'Unloaded' flattens the ongoing scene into a completed act; 'were unloaded' leaves a stray passive; 'have unloaded' changes the tense row.
practice.shortcut: were being + V3 → were + V-ing.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The school pays the bus driver well.'
options: The bus driver is pay well by the school.
The bus driver is being paid well by the school.
The bus driver are paid well by the school.
The bus driver is paid well by the school.
practice.solution: Simple present row → **is + V3**: *The bus driver is paid well by the school.* 'Is pay' drops the participle; 'is being paid' switches to the continuous row for a verb that is not continuous; 'are paid' fails the number of the driver.
practice.shortcut: Name the row first, then scan options for the broken cell.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The gardener is trimming the hedges.'
options: The hedges are trimmed by the gardener.
The hedges are being trim by the gardener.
The hedges is being trimmed by the gardener.
The hedges are being trimmed by the gardener.
practice.solution: Present continuous row → **are being trimmed by the gardener**. 'Are trimmed' reads as a routine, not the act in progress; 'are being trim' lacks the participle; 'is being trimmed' disagrees with the plural hedges.
practice.shortcut: -ing active → being + V3; then check number.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'Everyone respects a truthful man.'
options: A truthful man is respect by everyone.
A truthful man is respected by everyone.
A truthful man is being respected by everyone.
A truthful man was respected by everyone.
practice.solution: Simple present row → **A truthful man is respected by everyone**; here *everyone* is kept, since it carries meaning. 'Is respect' drops the participle; 'is being respected' imports a continuous the stem never had; 'was respected' changes the tense.
practice.shortcut: Everyone/people get dropped only when they add nothing.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The gardener was watering the plants at noon.'
options: The plants were being watered by the gardener at noon.
The plants were watered by the gardener at noon.
The plants are being watered by the gardener at noon.
The plants had been watered by the gardener at noon.
practice.solution: Past continuous row → **were being watered by the gardener at noon**. All three decoys are grammatical rows — of the WRONG tense: 'were watered' is simple past, 'are being watered' present continuous, 'had been watered' past perfect. Match the row, not the grammar.
practice.shortcut: Three clean-looking rows? Only one carries the right auxiliary.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'She sings patriotic songs on Independence Day.'
options: Patriotic songs are sung by her on Independence Day.
Patriotic songs are being sung by her on Independence Day.
Patriotic songs were sung by her on Independence Day.
Patriotic songs are sang by her on Independence Day.
practice.solution: Simple present row → **are sung by her on Independence Day**. 'Are being sung' adds a continuous; 'were sung' shifts to the past; 'are sang' uses the past form where the participle *sung* belongs.
practice.shortcut: sing-sang-sung: the passive always wants sung.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'They had already locked the gate before we reached.'
options: The gate has already been locked before we reached.
The gate was already being locked before we reached.
The gate had already being locked before we reached.
The gate had already been locked before we reached.
practice.solution: Past perfect row → **had already been locked**; the before-clause stays as it is. 'Has already been locked' upgrades the tense and clashes with the past clause; 'was already being locked' rewrites the row as past continuous; 'already being' puts being in a perfect slot.
practice.shortcut: had + V3 → had been + V3, adverbs stay put.

practice.q: Which one of the following sentences is in the passive voice?
options: The judge sentenced the thief to a fine.
The thief was sentenced to a fine by the judge.
The judge was sentencing the thief to a fine.
The judge has sentenced the thief to a fine.
practice.solution: *The thief was sentenced to a fine by the judge* shows the passive skeleton — **was + V3 with the receiver as subject and a by-agent**. The other three keep the judge before the verb; however their tenses differ, they are all active.
practice.shortcut: Passive test: does the receiver sit before be + V3?

practice.q: Which one of the following sentences is in the active voice?
options: The captain lifted the trophy.
The trophy was lifted by the captain.
The anthem was sung by the choir.
The gates were opened by the guard.
practice.solution: Only *The captain lifted the trophy* has the doer before a plain past verb — the active shape. The rest all show be + V3 with a by-phrase: receiver as subject, doer demoted — the passive skeleton in three costumes.
practice.shortcut: by-phrase + be + V3 = passive, every time.

practice.q: Choose the sentence that is NOT in the passive voice.
options: The packages have been delivered by the courier.
The courier has delivered the packages.
The parcels were being packed by the assistant.
The invoice was emailed to the client by the clerk.
practice.solution: *The courier has delivered the packages* keeps the doer in front of the verb — active. The other three all carry been/being + V3 with by-agents: have been delivered, were being packed, was emailed — passives all.
practice.shortcut: been or being + V3 → passive.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'They will have published the results by Friday.'
options: The results will be published by Friday.
The results will have published by Friday.
The results would have been published by Friday.
The results will have been published by Friday.
practice.solution: Future perfect row: **will have been + V3** — *The results will have been published by Friday.* 'Will be published' drops the perfect layer; 'will have published' leaves the results doing the publishing; 'would have been published' swaps the modal.
practice.shortcut: will have + V3 → will have been + V3.

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the question: 'Who has written this poem?'
options: By whom has this poem been written?
By whom this poem has been written?
Who has been written this poem?
By whom has this poem being written?
practice.solution: Who-doer question in the present perfect: **By whom + has + subject + been + V3** — *By whom has this poem been written?* The decoy with statement order drops the question inversion; 'Who has been written this poem' reverses the roles; 'being' cannot sit in a perfect slot.
practice.shortcut: Perfect + question: By whom has ... been + V3?

practice.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'We must not violate the traffic rules.'
options: The traffic rules must not be violated.
The traffic rules must not violated.
The traffic rules must not been violated.
The traffic rules could not be violated.
practice.solution: Modal + negative row: **must not be + V3** — *The traffic rules must not be violated.* The not sits between the modal and be. 'Must not violated' loses be; 'must not been violated' imports been where only be belongs; 'could not' silently softens the rule.
practice.shortcut: Modal row with not: modal + not + be + V3.
